Extract a SysML v2 model from the document as a list of facts. Each fact has unit_id (the sentence it comes from), type and slots. Give only the slots that have a value, as a list of {slot, value} pairs; for composition give one 'parts' pair per part.

Types and slots:
  attribute(owner,name,value,unit) action(performer,label) state(owner,label) constraint(subject,expression) requirement(subject,text)
  composition(whole,parts) flow(source,target,payload) succession(before,after) transition(from,to,trigger) allocation(action,to)

Name each element by its full name as first introduced in the document.
RULES:
- Resolve every entity-valued slot using all the text you are given. If a sentence refers to an element by an alias, abbreviation, pronoun or shorter description, write the element's full name as first introduced. If a sentence says an element receives or uses an item and the text you are given states which element produces or sends that item, emit a flow from that producer to the receiver. If an element cannot be determined from the text you are given, use null; never guess.
- Never write placeholder words such as "any", "all", "some state" for an unstated element; use null.
- Do not merge differently named things unless the text says they are the same.
- Emit one action for EVERY behavior verb phrase, including passive voice (performer null), capability statements, displays, logs, generates and reports. label = the verbatim verb phrase with its object.
- Emit a requirement for every NORMATIVE statement (shall, must, should, will, is required to, needs to). Purpose, goal or benefit sentences are not requirements.
- Emit a state for every named mode or state; transitions use the state names, with from null when the prior state is not stated.
- Emit a succession only for an EXPLICIT temporal connective between two actions ("then", "after", "once", "before", "when ... is complete", "next", "finally"); before/after are the action labels. Never use succession for cause or data transfer.
- Resolve a pronoun or "this/these" performer to the element named in the preceding sentence and write that element's name; if it cannot be resolved, use null. Never output a pronoun as a slot value.
- Drop determiners and quantifiers from element names ("Each Soil Moisture Probe" -> "Soil Moisture Probe", "the system" -> "system").
- allocation.to must be a component or actor, never a mode or state.
- Emit a constraint for every threshold, limit, period or deadline stated with a number; expression = the verbatim phrase.
- Emit a flow for every sentence in which an element sends, transmits, reports, displays, commands or delivers an item (target null if the receiver is not named).
 Also list under "entities" every system element, actor or item named in the document units, with its full name and any alias the text explicitly declares for it (e.g. 'hereafter X', 'known as X', 'called X'); aliases [] if none. Return JSON {"entities": [...], "facts": [...]}.

Memory from EARLIER parts of the document (do not extract facts from it; use it only to resolve names, aliases and who produces an item):
Document: Management by Trajectory (MBT) Concept of Operations (ConOps), far-term end-state vision for future air traffic management (ATM) in the National Airspace System (NAS). It is one interpretation of Trajectory Based Operations (TBO), consistent with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) TBO Concept Document, and is meant to guide research. Far-term means the NAS and most aircraft support Aeronautical Telecommunications Network-Baseline 2 (ATN-B2) data exchange; near- and far-term MBT differ in two ways. Current NAS: ATM automation predicts trajectories from the flight plan plus departure time; controllers issue uncommunicated 'open trajectory' clearances (tactical vectors/altitude/speed); Ground Delay Programs (GDPs) and Airspace Flow Programs (AFPs) assign departure times to meet a Controlled Time of Arrival (CTA); Time Based Flow Management (TBFM) assumes estimated times of arrival (ETAs) are correct; Traffic Flow Management (TFM) leaves reroutes to controllers. MBT: the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and airspace users (commercial, Unmanned Aircraft Systems, space vehicles, on-demand) negotiate closed four-dimensional trajectories (4DTs) from current state to destination for all Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) aircraft. All constraints are reflected in the 4DT; aircraft shall follow assigned 4DTs. The NAS Constraint Service publishes dynamic and static NAS constraints to all stakeholders and automation; trajectory constraints map to NAS constraints. Traffic management automation identifies flights affected by each traffic management initiative (TMI) and translates it into flight-specific trajectory constraints. Aircraft provide and share predicted 4DT (intent data) and send updates when it changes. Conflicts are detected earlier and resolved by adding/modifying 4DT constraints. Open trajectories are minimized by planning tactical maneuvers as closed modifications and by better predictability. Digital air-ground data communications deliver 4DTs to the cockpit Flight Management System (FMS); broadband links and electronic flight bag (EFB) apps include the flight crew in negotiation. Negotiating controller subsumes the D-side controller and, with traffic management coordinators (TMCs), proactively coordinates multi-sector 4DT changes. A time-based metric complements Performance Based Navigation (PBN), avoiding time of arrival control (TOAC) mixed equipage. Actors: FAA, airspace users, pilots/flight crew, controllers, TMCs, traffic management/ground/aircraft automation, NAS Constraint

Document units:
U0058: First, the near-term concept is constrained by the current NAS and currently planned changes to the NAS (i.e., changes that the FAA plans and are documented within the NAS Enterprise Architecture [EA] evolution within the NextGen timeframe), while the far-term concept may make assumptions about future enabling changes.
U0059: Second, while the far-term concept encompasses the entirety of air traffic control (ATC) within the NAS, in the near-term a more limited set of TBO operations may be feasible and beneficial. 1.5 Assumptions This section summarizes key assumptions about the near-term and far-term environments in which MBT would operate. 1.5.1 Assumptions about the Near-Term MBT Environment  Air traffic controllers will still be responsible for separation management and conflict avoidance; self-separation of IFR aircraft will not be the norm in the far-term MBT environment.  Air vehicle capabilities and equipage will be consistent with the current progression of safety and performance standards.  The capabilities of highly equipped aircraft will not change.
U0060: For example, aircraft FMS that include Required Time of Arrival (RTA) functionality will remain limited to a single active RTA constraint at a time.
U0061: Controller-pilot data link communications (CPDLC) with route clearances and trajectory intent output will be standard services supported by avionics.  MBT will slowly seep into NAS operations; there will not be a step change in procedures.
U0062: This will allow equipped aircraft to experience some benefit while operating among unequipped aircraft, and allow controllers with different perspectives on changing technologies and procedures to adapt to MBT at different paces.  MBT tools will be introduced incrementally through upgrades to existing automation platforms and extensions to the information shared via System Wide Information Management (SWIM).
U0063: Adoption of MBT will be varied around the NAS with some facilities and controllers more willing and able to adopt new capabilities than others.
U0064: Benefits will initially be slow to accumulate as controllers become more comfortable with the technologies.
U0065: Experience will allow the tools to be refined to improve performance and increase user acceptance.
U0066: Eventually, a critical mass of usage will be reached, resulting in increased usage and benefits.  Adoption of supporting technologies by airspace users will continue at its current pace.
